title: Experimental Investigation of Secondary Flow Structures Downstream of a Model Type IV Stent Failure in a 180° Curved Artery Test Section
protocol: Design stent models using CAD software.
Create straight stent geometry by defining parametric equations.
Initialize parameters for left and right helices in a Cartesian coordinate system.
Generate a set of 10 equi-spaced left turning helices in a planar circular array about a z-axis.
Repeat step 1.1.1 using Eq. 1, 2, 4 and 5 to generate a circular pattern of 10 equispaced left helices (Figure 1A).
Generate straight stent geometry by combining or assembling the left and right turning helices about a common axis (Figure 1A).

Create curved stent geometry by defining parametric equations and initializing parameters of the left and right helices in cylindrical (R-β-X) co-ordinate system or about a curved datum line (Table 1).
Repeat steps 1.1.1 - 1.1.2 with the previously initialized parameters using Eq. 1, 2, 6 and 7.
Generate a curved stent geometry combining or assembling the left and right turning helices curved about a common axis (R) and subtending an angle at the origin (Figure 1B).
Create high-resolution stereo lithography (STL) files from the straight and curved stent CAD models.
Select 'Export > Model' from the 'File menu'.
Choose 'STL' option.
Set 'chord height' to 0.
Set 'Angle control' to 1.
Apply 'OK' to create the STL-file.
Fabricate stent models on a rapid prototyping machine.
Start the 3D printing software.
Insert the STL-file located on the 3D-printer computer.
Place the 3D rendering of the STL-file on a virtual platform ('Tray') on the screen.
Select units as 'mm' from the file menu tabs.
Select the quality of finished product as 'Matte'.
Select 'Tray settings > Validation' tab to validate the model.
Look for the 'Validation succeeded' message to proceed.
If validation is unsuccessful, repeat steps until successful validation is achieved.
Select 'Tray settings > Build' tab to send the file to the 3D-printer for fabrication.
Pour 500 ml of deionized H₂O into a 2,000 ml beaker.
Place the beaker on the magnetic stirrer.
Measure approximately 860 g of NaI and add it in increments of 100 g to the beaker while stirring until fully dissolved before adding more.
Record the temperature at each addition of NaI.
Refrigerate the solution if necessary to maintain room temperature (≈25°C).
Add small increments of NaI (approximately 5-10 g) up to a total of 20 g, until the solution is saturated.
Measure and record the mass and temperature of each addition.
Remove the beaker with the saturated NaI solution from the magnetic stirrer when done.
Measure the density of the saturated NaI solution.
Add 10 ml of saturated NaI solution to a 50 ml beaker on a zeroed-scale using a syringe or volumetric pipette, ensuring there are no air bubbles.
Record the mass and volume added.
Calculate the density of each addition using Equation 8.
Repeat this step about 4-5 times.
Average the densities recorded.
Return the solution to the batch of saturated NaI solution prepared in step 2.1.
Measure the mass of the saturated NaI solution prepared in step 2.1.
Calculate its volume using Equation 9.
Estimate the total volume of the blood mimicking solution.
Estimate the partial volumes of glycerol and deionized water to be added following Equations 10, 11, and 12.
Prepare a blood analog solution comprising of 79% saturated NaI solution, 20% glycerol, and 1% deionized water by volume through homogenized mixing on a magnetic stirrer.
Place the beaker with the saturated NaI solution on the magnetic stirrer.
Add glycerol in small increments until the entire volume is added.
Record the volume added for each increment and wait until the solution is visibly homogenized before adding the next increment.
After complete homogenization, add blood-analog fluid using a syringe or pipette.
Continue stirring until the blood-analog solution is visibly homogenized.
Measure the kinematic viscosity using a Ubbelohde viscometer or equivalent instrument.
Adjust the kinematic viscosity by adding small quantities of glycerol if necessary.
Measure the refractive index using a refractometer.
Adjust the refractive index by adding minute quantities of sodium thiosulfate anhydrous using a spatula.
Install stents fabricated in step 1 in the curved artery test section made of acrylic to embody an idealized Type IV fracture scenario.
Place the straight stent upstream of the curved artery test section.
Ensure a spacing between the straight and the curved stents that is 3 times the diameter of the tube (12.7 mm).
Place one end of the 45° curved stent at the inlet to the curved tube inside the curvature.
Connect the straight acrylic pipes to the inlet and outlet of the 180° curved artery test section.
Assemble the experimental setup on an optical table.
Place the laser sheet at the 90° location for secondary flow velocity field acquisition.
Use particle image velocimetry (PIV) technique to acquire secondary flow velocity fields.
Turn on the laser using the ON/OFF switches located on the laser power source.
Illuminate a small piece of paper to visualize the laser sheet.
Adjust the laser sheet thickness to approximately 2 mm visually, by turning the laser sheet focusing optics located on the laser source.
Place the laser sheet along the 90° measurement region so that the sheet is perpendicular to the optical table.
Place the camera near the 0° or 180° location to gain optical access to the cross-sectional view illuminated by the laser sheet.

Align laser and camera using the image acquisition and post processing software to adjust the field of view of the camera to sufficiently capture the image of the circular cross-section of the curved artery and reducing the particle distortion.
Switch off the laser using the control switches located on the laser power source.
Make sure that the camera is turned on with the lens cover removed.
Start image acquisition and post processing software on the PIV data acquisition computer and log in as 'expert user'.
Create a new project from the file menu, specify a 'Project name' and select 'PIV' option under the 'Type of project'.
Select 'New' from the file menu to initialize a new PIV recording session.
Select 'Device' under 'Settings' section on image acquisition and post processing software.
Navigate to 'Recording' dialogue box on the screen.
Activate 'Camera 1' check box.
Select 'Single Frame (T1A)' option.
Select laser 'radio button' to be set to ON in the image acquisition and post processing software settings.
Activate external power mode on the laser power source by pressing 'EXT' and 'High power' switches.
Select 'Grab' on the image acquisition and post processing software to start acquiring PIV images.
Move camera with slight manual adjustments on the optical table.
Adjust focus to optimize the location of the camera to maximize field-of-view, reduce blurriness and image distortion.
Select 'Stop' radio button on image acquisition and post processing software settings to cease acquiring PIV data.
Do not make any further camera adjustments.
Turn on the programmable pump using the ON/OFF switch located on the pump.
Launch the instrument control program on the pump instrument control computer.
Load the text-file containing voltage-time waveform values with a reference trigger (t/T = 0) into the instrument control software.
Set 'Amplitude' to 1 Volt in the instrument control software interface screen.
Set 'DC offset' to 0 Volts in the instrument control software interface screen.
Set 'Number of time steps' to 1,000 in the instrument control software interface screen.
Set 'Time period' to 4 seconds in the instrument control software interface screen.
Confirm that the external power mode on the laser power source is activated.
Press the 'EXT' switch located on the laser power source if required.
Press the 'High power' switch located on the laser power source if required.
Select 'Device' after clicking 'New Recording' under the 'Settings' section in the image acquisition and post processing software.
Navigate to the 'Recording' dialogue box, activate 'Camera 1' check box, and select 'Double Frame (T1A+T1B)' option on the image acquisition and post processing software.
Select 'Timing' option on the 'Recording' dialogue box, set 'Trigger source' to 'External cyclic trigger', and synchronize with trigger-signals from the pump instrument control module.
Select 'Aquisit' under the 'Settings' section to start setting up PIV acquisition.
Navigate to the 'Recording sequence' dialogue box on the image acquisition and post processing software.
Add a 'Table scan' subcategory under 'Recording sequence'.
Populate the table using 'Edit Table scan', 'Append Scan', input time values starting from 0 milliseconds and ending at 4,000 milliseconds in intervals of 40 milliseconds.
Input Δt-values corresponding to each time entry in the table.
Press 'Enter' on the keyboard after every value entered.
Navigate to the 'Recording sequence' dialogue box.
Add 'Image Acquisition' subcategory under 'Table scan'.
Set the 'Number of images' to 200.
Activate the check box 'Show images while recording'.
Select 'Start immediately'.
Select 'Device' under the 'Settings' section.
Confirm that the laser is set to 'ON' with appropriate power settings.
Navigate to 'Laser Control' to confirm.
Select the 'RUN' radio button on instrument control software interface.
Supply fluid to the experiment using inputs from steps 4.8.2-4.8.3.
Provide a trigger pulse every 4 seconds.
Select 'Start Recording'.
Acquire phase-wise measurements using trigger-signal from pump instrument control.
Stop recording once 200 planar velocity fields are acquired at each time instance.
Press 'Stop' on the laser power source.
Turn off the pump and camera.
Place the camera lens cover.
Select 'Stop' radio button on instrument control software interface.
Visually inspect experimental setup to gage the level of leakage.
Gather leaked fluid if necessary.
Ensure all devices have been powered off or can be left on standby.
Close the recording session in the image acquisition software.
Close the recording session in the post-processing software.
Create a mask that encompasses the internal flow geometry.
Select the project created in step 4.4 containing PIV data.
Follow instructions in "Supplemental Code File - creating a mask".
Populate 'Operation list' dialogue box with steps from "Supplemental Code File - creating a post processing routine".
Compute phase-averaged secondary flow velocity fields.
Compute R.M.S. secondary flow velocity fields.
Compute vorticity fields.
Select the operation 'vector statistics: vector field result'.
Activate 'Average V' and 'RMS V' check boxes under the 'Vector fields' section.
Select the operation 'rot-z Eyx - Exy' from the group 'extract scalar field: rotation and shear'.
Start post processing the entire PIV data.
Generate phase-averaged quantities of velocity, R.M.S velocity, vorticity and swirling strength using previously created operations.
Right-click on any PIV data under the project window.
Select 'HyperLoop > All sets'.
Select option 'Add all' under the 'Available Sets:' section.
Select 'Parameter' from the pull down menu under the 'Filter:' section.
Select 'Batch Processing' option under the 'Operation:' section.
Click 'Execute' to start 'hyperloop' post processing of the PIV data.
Select the operation 'swirling strength' from the group 'extract scalar field: rotation and shear'.
Repeat steps 5.4.1-5.4.2 to execute ‘Hyperloop’ post-processing.
Detect coherent structures using continuous wavelet transform on vorticity field.
Create user-defined MATLAB functions for the detection process.
Use PIVmat 3.01-based MATLAB functions to perform analysis.
Generate a 2D array of data from a given equation.
Initialize the scale factor in Eq. 13 to an arbitrary value.
Perform two-dimensional convolution or Fourier multiplication with vorticity data and Ricker wavelet function.
Generate wavelet transformed vorticity field at initialized scale factor.
Compute Shannon entropy of the wavelet transformed vorticity field.
Change the scale factor.
Generate a new 2D array representing the 2D Ricker wavelet.
Repeat steps for a large range of scale factors.
Create a plot of Shannon entropy vs. wavelet scale factor.
Locate an optimal wavelet scale corresponding to a local minimum in Shannon entropy.
Repeat step at optimum wavelet scale.
Create a contour plot of the wavelet transformed vorticity at the optimal wavelet scale factor.
